Bluetooth Low Energy, from the radio up · Puzzle 1 · 2 of 5

Shouting into the room

In puzzle 0, the strap's radio slept almost all the time. Here's how a device that's nearly always asleep still gets found.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 0: A year on a coin battery

    The radio is the hungriest part of a small device. BLE keeps it off almost all the time and wakes it only for short, planned moments. Every rule in this course follows from that.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 1 puzzle: 0. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

In puzzle 0, the strap's radio slept almost all the time to save its battery. But you open an app, and your phone finds the strap in a second or two. How does a phone find something that's nearly always asleep?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

The strap is loud only for moments. It wakes, sends a packet, one short burst of data, that says "I'm a heart strap, here's my name", listens for a moment in case someone answers (puzzle 2 uses that), and goes back to sleep. Doing that over and over is advertising.

The time between two advertisements is the advertising interval: at least 20 ms, and it can be seconds or much longer. Short means found fast; long means a longer battery life. To every interval the radio adds a random delay of 0 to 10 ms. Two packets sent at the same moment on the same channel garble each other: a collision. If two straps happened to start together, the random delays make them drift apart instead of colliding every time.

BLE splits its airwaves into 40 channels, like stations on a radio dial: a radio sends or listens on one at a time. Advertising uses only 3 of them, and each advertisement is sent on all 3, one after another. Three is few enough that a listener knows where to listen, and more than one, so noise on a single channel (another radio, like Wi-Fi, sending on the same slice) doesn't hide the strap.

Your phone, meanwhile, is scanning: listening on the advertising channels. It can't hear all three at once, so it listens on one for a while, then the next. Because the strap repeats every interval on all three, sooner or later one of its packets lands on the channel the phone is listening to, and the phone hears it.

The analogy

The lighthouse from puzzle 0 flashes its lamp in three directions, one after another, anything from many times a second to every few seconds. A ship's lookout watches one direction at a time. Sooner or later, a flash lands where the lookout is looking.

Check yourself

You shorten a strap's advertising interval from 1 s to 100 ms. What changes?

Right. Advertise often to be found fast; rarely to last long.

Not quite. More advertisements give the phone more chances to hear one, so finding gets faster.

Not quite. Every advertisement wakes the radio. Ten times as many means ten times the radio time.

Why does each advertisement go out on three channels, not one?

Not quite. Any one copy is enough. The other two are backups against noise.

Right. Few enough to find, more than one to survive noise.

Not quite. It's the same packet three times, on three channels.

What's the difference between advertising and scanning?

Not quite. They're the two sides: one shouts, the other listens.

Right. One side shouts, the other listens.

Not quite. Scanning here is listening, not sending: the phone hears advertisements.

Sources

  • Bluetooth Core Specification 5.4, Vol 6, Part B: Link Layer ("40 RF channels are defined… divided into 3 RF channels known as the 'primary advertising channels'… and 37 RF channels known as the 'general-purpose channels'"; "The advertising interval (advInterval) shall be an integer multiple of 0.625 ms in the range 20 ms to 10,485.759375 s. The advDelay is a (pseudo-)random value with a range 0 ms to 10 ms"; "When scanning, the Link Layer shall listen on the primary advertising physical channel")

What you now know

A device advertises: it wakes, sends a short packet on each of the 3 advertising channels, and sleeps, over and over at its advertising interval. A phone scans: it listens on those channels until one packet lands while it's listening.
